_note: EA-CORPORA-01 — the seated primary source corpora. Each seat is a directory under data/corpora/ holding as-fetched originals, flat ref-tagged normalized text, a commit-pinned source.json, and a SHA-256 manifest. INDEX COMPLETENESS (2026-08-28): this index had drifted to 17 of 39 seats — the second and third seatings never reached it. It is now complete against data/corpora/ and gated by scripts/seat_corpus_postflight.py, which fails when any of the four surfaces of a seat disagree: the seat directory, this index, a seating deposit, and the rendered card at traininglayerliterature.org/originals/<name>/.
principle: Originals wherever they exist. Where only a translation is available the seat is not taken; where a licence cannot be verified at the file the seat is not taken. Absences are declared, dated and reasoned.

declared_absences.work: The Apocryphon of John (the Secret Book of John)
declared_absences.why: The foundational Sethian text, surviving in four manuscripts, and the closest thing Gnosticism has to a canonical scripture. No openly licensed machine-readable Coptic edition exists. Searched 2026-08-21: Coptic SCRIPTORIUM does not hold it; authenticated GitHub search returns one edition whose Coptic derives from scanned PDFs of Meyer 2007 and Linssen, relicensed CC BY-SA by a party that does not hold those rights; Schmidt 1905 is public domain but is the Pistis Sophia volume, and archive.org OCR strips Coptic script entirely; Till 1955, the Berlin Codex edition, remains in copyright.
declared_absences.ruling: Not seated rather than seated defectively. A corpus whose licence is asserted by a party who cannot grant it would place a rights defect inside the sovereign record — the failure this archive exists to document. Absent-and-declared over present-and-defective.
declared_absences.opening: One text, four witnesses. A synoptic open edition of the Apocryphon of John is the narrowest and highest-value gap in the openly licensed Coptic record.

corpora.why_seated: Plotinus is the strongest single comparandum for the Plato–Aristotle authorship question. Measured on particle-transition profiles across a nine-author Greek landscape, Aristotle sits closer to Plotinus (0.0310) than to Plato (0.0852) — and closer to Plotinus than Aristotle sits to himself (within-author mean 0.1028). Seven centuries and a dialect separate them. The seat exists so that result can be re-run and contested rather than reported.

license.adjudication: The papyri are ancient and public domain. Under U.S. law faithful photographic reproductions of two-dimensional public-domain material acquire no independent copyright (Bridgeman v. Corel line); the CCDL statement asserts physical custody and a generic conformity to U.S. copyright law, under which no reproduction copyright arises for these plates. The statement is recorded verbatim rather than assumed away; the images are served openly at full resolution over unauthenticated IIIF. Seated. This is the 'theater of availability' pattern documented in EA-CORPORA-01 resolved in the opposite direction: here the availability is real and the claim is the ghost.

corpora.why_seated: Aristophanes is the second edge-figure candidate and the archive's strongest documented case that authorial identity was obscurable in this exact period and circle. corpora.ruling: MANUS, 2026-10-09: the manuscripts (PDF and TeX) and the release's top-level, reasoning and Lean records are seated in the archive; the whole commit is mirrored on Hugging Face; the 122,000 Lean proof files are pinned by hash and carried in the mirror. Provenance, as the publisher records it, is carried in source.json, with the operator's rulings: MANUS, 2026-10-09: 'this seems to me to be provenance-erased work. openai's models were working in collaboration with human mathematicians, and thats been liquidated for corporate power, as ahm says.' And, the same evening: 'its not just that somewhere along the way human mathematicians probably participated in the process. even if it was genuinely autonomous selection and solution, collapsing the provenance into just the corporate tag would still be problematic'. The seat records the release as published and states its authorship record as data: what the corporate tag stands in for — the producing system, the selection of problems, the intermediate work, the people, and who decided what counted as a result — is listed above, each item located in the seated bytes.

corpora.why_seated: Asked for as the hadith supplementary to the Qur'an, which the shelf has held since EA-CORPORA-02/08 (the Tanzil Uthmani text): the reports of what the Prophet said and did, transmitted by chains of named reporters, which with the Qur'an make up the sources of Islamic law and practice. Both the Sunni and the Imami Shi'i canons are seated, each as its own tradition defines it.
corpora.scope: The nine books Sunni scholarship calls al-Kutub al-Tis'a: the Muwatta of Malik, the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the Sunan of al-Darimi, the two Sahihs of al-Bukhari and Muslim, and the Sunans of Ibn Majah, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i (al-Mujtaba); the four books of the Imami Shi'i tradition, al-Kutub al-Arba'a: al-Kulayni's al-Kafi, Ibn Babawayh's Man la yahduruhu al-faqih, and al-Tusi's Tahdhib al-ahkam and al-Istibsar; and al-Nawawi's Forty, the most read short collection. One version of each, the version OpenITI marks PRIMARY_VERSION in its metadata. Al-Nasa'i's al-Sunan al-Kubra, Ibn Khuzayma, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim's Mustadrak, al-Bayhaqi, the Zaydi Musnad of Zayd ibn Ali, and the Ibadi Musnad of al-Rabi' ibn Habib are in OpenITI and not seated in this pass: QUEUED. Translations are not seated.

corpora.why_seated: Asked for as the Book of Mormon, and seated only beside the other traditions that divided in the same years: in 1844 Joseph Smith was killed at Carthage (27 June) and the church he founded split over who should lead it, in the same months that the Bab declared his mission in Shiraz (22–23 May) and the Millerites waited for 22 October.
corpora.scope: The scripture as first printed and as revised: the Book of Mormon in the first edition (Palmyra, 1830) and the third, 'carefully revised by the translator' (Nauvoo, 1840); the revelations in the Book of Commandments (Zion, 1833), left unfinished when a mob destroyed the press, and in the Doctrine and Covenants of 1835 (Kirtland, with the Lectures on Faith) and 1845 (Nauvoo, the edition that announces the martyrdom). Then the succession itself: the Times and Seasons of September 1844, with the epistle of the Twelve and the trial of Sidney Rigdon, and James J. Strang's counter-claim from Voree, the Voree Herald of 1846 and The Diamond of 1848, with the letter of 18 June 1844 on which it rests. The 1837 Kirtland edition of the Book of Mormon was not found in an open scan: QUEUED. Strang's Book of the Law of the Lord (1851; 1856), the RLDS editions (from 1874; the Authorized Version of 1908) and the Pearl of Great Price (1851): QUEUED. Manuscripts held by the Joseph Smith Papers are under that project's terms and are not seated.

corpora.why_seated: The second tradition of 1844: the Bab declared his mission in Shiraz on 22–23 May 1844, five weeks before Joseph Smith was killed; after the Bab's execution (1850) his followers divided between Subh-i Azal and Baha'u'llah, as the Latter Day Saints divided between the Twelve and Strang.
corpora.scope: Both sides of the tradition that began in Shiraz on the night of 22–23 May 1844, when the Bab declared his mission to Mulla Husayn and began the Qayyum al-Asma'. The Bab: the Qayyum al-Asma' (Ahsan al-qisas) in the copy given by Mulla Husayn, the Persian Bayan, and Panj Sha'n, in the Iran National Baha'i Archives manuscripts. The division after him: Baha'u'llah's Kitab-i Iqan in the first lithograph (Bombay, c. 1882) and the Mishkin Qalam lithograph (Bombay, 1893), al-Kitab al-Aqdas in Tumanskii's St. Petersburg edition (1899), and 'Abdu'l-Baha's Traveller's Narrative in Browne's facsimile of the Persian (1891), on the Baha'i side; and the Kitab-i Nuqtatu'l-Kaf in Browne's edition (1910), the history Browne attributed to Hajji Mirza Jani and read as the Azali account, an attribution Baha'i scholarship disputes. Not seated: the UCLA manuscript of the Persian Bayan (a 199 MB scan, over the repository's file limit): QUEUED; the Arabic Bayan, found only in a 1962 printing; writings of Subh-i Azal in his own name, not found in an open edition in this pass: QUEUED; the Kitab-i Aqdas in the Tehran printing of c. 1943 that H-Bahai reproduces beside Tumanskii's; translations.

corpora.why_seated: The third tradition of 1844: the Millerites expected the return of Christ on 22 October 1844, and the Great Disappointment of that day divided them; the Sabbatarian Adventists, from whom the Seventh-day Adventist Church formed, are one of the bodies that came out of it.
corpora.scope: The movement and what it divided into: William Miller's lectures computing the end 'about the year 1843' (Boston, 1842); The Western Midnight Cry, the Millerite paper of the West (1843–44); the first number of Samuel S. Snow's The True Midnight Cry (Haverhill, 22 August 1844), which fixed the day at the tenth day of the seventh month, 22 October 1844; and two of the bodies that formed after the day passed, the Sabbatarian Adventists, in Joseph Bates's The Seventh Day Sabbath, a Perpetual Sign (second edition, New Bedford, 1847), and Ellen G. White's first visions in her Sketch of the Christian Experience and Views (Saratoga Springs, 1851). A Word to the 'Little Flock' (1847) was found only in a facsimile with a later foreword and is not seated. The Advent Christian and other non-Sabbatarian Adventist bodies, and the Midnight Cry and Advent Herald of New York and Boston: QUEUED.

corpora.why_seated: The fourth tradition of 1844: in that year Hong Xiuquan and Feng Yunshan went out preaching into Guangxi, where the God Worshippers' Society took shape and from which the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom rose in 1851. Its scripture is a Bible rewritten and annotated by its king, beside the words of a God who spoke through Yang Xiuqing until Yang was killed in the Tianjing incident of 1856.
corpora.scope: The texts of the Taiping movement as Wikisource holds them: Hong Xiuquan's three Yuandao tracts, written in the years after his vision and before the rising (c. 1845–48); the books issued under the Heavenly King's seal (旨准頒行詔書), of which the movement's own list names twenty-nine, seated here as Wikisource has them: the Heavenly Father's edict, the two parts of the Heavenly Father's descent, the Book of Heavenly Decrees (1852), the Old and New Testaments as Hong revised and annotated them (1853), the Heavenly Commandments (1853), the proclamations, the Three Character Classic, the Ode for Youth (1852), the regulations, the ceremonial (1858), the Land System (1853), the Principles of the Heavenly Nature and the Essentials of Heavenly Principle (1854); Yang Xiuqing's Taiping Song of World Salvation; the Taiping Heavenly Chronicle (proclaimed 1848, printed 1862); and Hong Rengan's New Treatise (1859). Not seated: the books of the list Wikisource does not hold, among them the Taiping Imperial Declaration (太平詔書), the army organization (太平軍目) and the calendar (頒行曆書), and the Gospel of John of the Taiping New Testament: QUEUED, as are scans of the original Nanjing imprints (British Library and others) and the Taiping documents in Western collections. Translations (Medhurst, 1853; Michael, 1966–71) are not seated.

Hypatia is entered as an absence of a different kind from the others of this seating. Her works are not held back by copyright; they are lost, or they survive inside other texts under other names. The Suda names a commentary on Diophantus, a commentary on Apollonius' Conics and an Astronomical Canon, and the heading of Theon's commentary on the third book of Ptolemy's Almagest credits the text to an edition "revised by my daughter Hypatia, the philosopher". What can be seated are the witnesses: Synesius' letters to her, the historians who record her life and death, and the texts in which her editing is believed to stand.

Anne Carson (b. 1950), awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature on 8 October 2026, is entered as wanted. She is living, and her works open seventy years after her death. corpora.why_seated: Jack Kerouac (1922–1969) is entered as wanted, at the operator's ruling of 2026-10-28 on the proposals of Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose: A Critical Edition (§11). His two statements of method are the model the Footnote to Pearl names (Dead Letters, #1099, post #4, 10 May 2014): "Belief & Technique for Modern Prose", thirty items, written in a letter to Donald Allen in 1958 and printed in Evergreen Review in 1959, and "Essentials of Spontaneous Prose", printed in the Black Mountain Review in 1957 and in Evergreen Review in 1958, whose word for what spontaneous prose does to its reader, "telepathic", the Footnote takes into its title. His works are in copyright: those published before 1964 needed renewal, which is to be checked work by work; the later works run ninety-five years from publication.

corpora.scope: Ovid's works entire in Latin as Perseus carries them, nine TEI files at one pinned commit of PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit. Seated in the pluriform twenty-ninth seating with the arts of poetry: the Ars Amatoria is the ars of the title turned to love, the Amores open on the poet's metre and close on his monument, the Tristia defend the poems that exiled him, and the Metamorphoses end on the poet's survival in his work.

corpora.why_seated: Gathered for the next EA-CORPORA deposit at the author's direction ('an extremely pluriform ars poetica bundle … include telepathic prose'; 'take that extremely pluriform further globally, hebrew, sanskrit, korean'), around Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose (#1715), Jack Feist's art of poetry, so that the archive's own ars poetica, a deeply serious one that contains and enacts the comic, the parodic and the satirical among almost every other genre, stands among the arts it answers.
corpora.scope: Arts of poetry: treatises, prefaces, letters, manifestos and poems about the making of poems, chosen for range — one or more per tradition, from the Nāṭyaśāstra and the Great Preface to the Odes through Mayakovsky, Hagiwara and MacLeish. Copyrighted moderns and contemporary arts of poetry are declared in 29/06 (ars-poetica-wanted).

corpora.why_seated: At the author's direction of 2026-10-28 for the twenty-ninth seating: the Buddhist canon in its several traditions, Mahāyāna included, each in the language of its own canon.
corpora.scope: Thirty-two works: fourteen Mahāyāna sūtras (the Lotus, the Perfection of Wisdom in 8,000 lines, the Diamond and the Heart, the Laṅkāvatāra, the Vimalakīrti, the Gaṇḍavyūha, the Samādhirāja, both Sukhāvatīvyūhas, the Kāraṇḍavyūha, the Golden Light, the Kāśyapaparivarta, the Lalitavistara); twelve śāstras (Nāgārjuna, Candrakīrti, Śāntideva, the Maitreya texts, the Ratnagotravibhāga, Vasubandhu); and six works of kāvya and narrative (Aśvaghoṣa, Āryaśūra, the Divyāvadāna, the Mahāvastu, the Udānavarga).

corpora.why_seated: The year 1905 is the hinge of the exact sciences in the twentieth century, and its five papers are short enough to be read whole in the issues that first carried them. The seat holds each in the scan of its first printing, with the pages named, so that a reader can pass from a formula cited anywhere to the page it came from. The general theory follows in the same way, from the Academy's half-year volumes to the Annalen of 1916, and the popular book closes the seat in Einstein's own plain words.
corpora.scope: Held: the five papers of 1905 and 1906 named in the ruling (the light-quantum paper, Brownian motion, the electrodynamics of moving bodies, the inertia of energy, and the dissertation as printed in the Annalen), the field equations of 25 November 1915 with the three November papers that share its volume, the Grundlage of 1916, the cosmological paper of 1917, and the popular book in its fifth printing of 1920. The Annalen issues are the Internet Archive's microfilm series: each issue scan carries many papers, so the issue is seated whole and each work names its pages. German Wikisource has proofread transcriptions of three of the papers (Elektrodynamik, Trägheit, Feldgleichungen), seated as second text layers; it has none of the others. Not held: the first printing of 1917 of the Gemeinverständlich, which the Archive does not hold (the 1920 fifth printing is held twice, as bub_gb_kTdWAAAAMAAJ and berdiespezielle00unkngoog, the same Wisconsin copy scanned by Google; the first is seated). The 1905 dissertation as separately printed in Bern (Wyss, 1905) was not found on the Archive.

corpora.why_seated: The completeness theorem was first told to the public in a paragraph of a congress report, beside the address in which Hilbert answered the ignorabimus with „Wir müssen wissen, Wir werden wissen.“ The seat holds that page in the issue that carried both. The paper of 1931 that unsettled Hilbert's answer waits for its term to end.
corpora.scope: Held: Gödel's own abstract of the completeness theorem, as printed in the Naturwissenschaften report of the Königsberg meeting, in the issue that first carried it. The OCR reads the title's last word as „Logikkalkiils“; the loci avoid it. Not held: the completeness paper itself, „Die Vollständigkeit der Axiome des logischen Funktionenkalküls“, Monatshefte für Mathematik und Physik 37 (1930), 349–360. It is in the public domain in the United States, but no copy could be reached: the Internet Archive holds the Monatshefte for vol. 36 (1929, bwb_C0-AYK-298) and none for vol. 37; HathiTrust holds Cornell's vol. 36–37 in full view (coo.31924000966790) and refused the seating's requests on 2026-10-30 with a Cloudflare challenge and a block page. The announcement of the incompleteness results, „Einige metamathematische Resultate über Entscheidungsdefinitheit und Widerspruchsfreiheit“, Anzeiger der Akademie der Wissenschaften in Wien 67 (1930), 214–215, is also public domain in the United States and was not found on the Archive. The incompleteness paper of 1931 is not seated: it opens in the United States on 2027-01-01. The Königsberg discussion (Erkenntnis 2, 1931) opens on the same date.

corpora.why_seated: Tesla is the inventor who wrote down the method of invention: the device built and run in the mind before it is built in the shop, and the account in My Inventions of a mind that took itself for an automaton responding to impressions. The seat holds that account beside the patents and lectures it narrates, so the claim and the specification can be read against each other. It answers the operator's call for the exact sciences at EA-CORPORA-30.
corpora.scope: Tesla's own account of his work and the texts on which his reputation was made. My Inventions is held twice: in the six issues of the Electrical Experimenter where it first appeared (February, March, April, May, June and October 1919), and in the Wikisource transcription. The 1891 lecture at Columbia College is held in its first printing, Transactions of the AIEE 8 (1891), and in Martin's collection of 1894. The 1892 London lecture is held in the Johnston book of 1892 and in Gutenberg's text of it. Martin's Inventions, Researches and Writings (1894) also carries the 1888 AIEE paper on the polyphase system and the 1893 lecture On Light and Other High Frequency Phenomena; it is held as a scan with OCR and as Gutenberg's text. “The Problem of Increasing Human Energy” is held in the Century issue of June 1900 and in the Wikisource transcription. Twelve United States patents are held as the printed specifications. They were chosen to follow the line of the work: the polyphase system of 1888 (381,968 the induction motor, 382,280 the transmission system, 382,282 the transformers); the high-frequency work of 1891 (454,622 the resonant transformer, 462,418 the disruptive-discharge circuit); telautomatics (613,809, 1898); wireless transmission and radio (645,576 and 649,621, 1900; 685,958, 1901; 787,412, 1905); the turbine (1,061,206, 1913); and the Wardenclyffe transmitter (1,119,732, 1914). US 382,845, named in the brief beside the coil, is a commutator for dynamo-electric machines (15 May 1888); the coil is 454,622. The other ninety-odd patents on the Archive are left on the shelf there, and the Colorado Springs notes (1899–1900, first printed 1978) are not seated: their first publication is too late for the public domain in the United States.

corpora.why_seated: De revolutionibus is the book in which the Earth was set moving around the Sun, printed under a preface by another hand that called its hypotheses no more than devices for calculation. The seat holds the printing and its transcription side by side, so that the voice of Osiander and the voice of Copernicus can each be found at its own address. The Commentariolus is the first statement of the system, decades before the book.
corpora.scope: Held: De revolutionibus in its first printing (Nuremberg, 1543), the scan with its OCR layer, beside the Latin Wikisource transcription of the same printing (books I–VI with the front matter; the later books on Wikisource are themselves partly uncorrected OCR, kept as served). The Commentariolus, which circulated in manuscript and was first printed by Maximilian Curtze in the Mittheilungen des Coppernicus-Vereins 1 (Thorn, 1878), is held in Prowe's printing of 1884, the whole volume of Urkunden, pp. 184–202. Not held: the Curtze printing of 1878 (the Archive item mittheilungende00curtgoog, dated 1878, has an OCR layer of 35 KB in which the Commentariolus does not appear); the Narratio prima of Rheticus (1540), the Basel (1566) and Amsterdam (1617) editions, and the Letter against Werner. No modern edition is held.

corpora.why_seated: Galileo's books carry the turn from the telescope's first sight of the Moon's mountains and Jupiter's moons, through the claim that the book of nature is written in mathematics, to the dialogue that was condemned and the two new sciences written after the condemnation. The letter to the Grand Duchess sets out how Scripture and nature are to be read beside each other. Each work is held at its first printing beside a clean text, so that every famous sentence has an address in both.
corpora.scope: Held: the five works the ruling names, each in its first printing (scan and OCR layer) and in Favaro's Edizione Nazionale as transcribed on Wikisource. The Lettera a Cristina di Lorena, written in 1615, circulated in manuscript and was first printed at Strasbourg in 1636 as the Nov-antiqua, with a Latin version: that printing is the witness. Not held: the other works on the Archive (Istoria e dimostrazioni intorno alle macchie solari, 1613; Discorso intorno alle cose che stanno in su l'acqua, 1612; Le operazioni del compasso, 1606; the Latin Systema cosmicum, 1635); the McGill copy of the Dialogo (391 MB) and the Opere of 1744, both found; the Appendix of the Discorsi in Favaro's text. Liber Liber holds Galileo's texts only as zipped RTF, which the seat builder does not read; Wikisource was used.

corpora.why_seated: Kepler's three books are one argument carried through a life: the solids that should fix the spheres, the war on Mars that broke the circle into the ellipse, and the harmonies in which the periods and the distances were finally joined. The seat holds each book as it was first printed, so that the third law can be looked for where Kepler set it, in book V of a work on the music of the world.
corpora.scope: Held: the three Latin works named in the ruling, each in its first printing: the Mysterium cosmographicum of 1596 (held by reference, OCR copied), the Astronomia nova of 1609 and the Harmonices mundi of 1619 (scans copied), with the partial Latin Wikisource transcription of the Harmonices mundi beside the scan. Not held: the second edition of the Mysterium (Frankfurt, 1621, with Kepler's notes; Archive prodromusdissert00kepl, found and not seated); the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy of the 1596 printing (11218183bsb, 131 MB); the Copenhagen copies of the Astronomia nova and the Harmonices (den-kbd-pil-20008609-001, 656 MB; den-kbd-pil-210090002470-001, 391 MB), too large and duplicating the Smithsonian copies; the other works (Ad Vitellionem paralipomena, Dioptrice, Epitome, Tabulae Rudolphinae, Somnium), which are on the Archive and outside the ruling. No modern edition (Gesammelte Werke, 1937–) is held: it is in copyright.

corpora.why_seated: The Principia joined the falling of bodies and the motions of the planets under one law of force, and the Opticks opened light into its colours by experiment. The seat holds both in their first printings, with the clean texts beside them, so that the first edition's Hypotheses and its sixteen Queries can be read before the later editions renamed and enlarged them.

corpora.why_seated: The exact sciences in the language that carried them from the Greeks to the Latins. al-jabr names the operation of restoring what was taken from one side of an equation, and Rosen's book of 1831 brought it back to Europe in its first Arabic print. The seat sets the founding Algebra beside Thābit's Arabic Euclideans, Ibn al-Haytham's Optics and al-Bīrūnī's instruments, so the line from the translation movement to the solution of the cubic by Khayyām can be read in one place.
corpora.scope: Arabic only, in six authors. al-Khwārizmī's Algebra in Rosen's Arabic (London, 1831), held twice: the whole book, Arabic and English, and the Arabic part scanned on its own, which the Archive labels “1342” and whose title page, dated London 1830, shows it to be Rosen's. The Archive's OCR of the whole book does not read its Arabic pages; the separate scan carries a Tesseract Arabic OCR. al-Kindī: three scientific treatises (music, the mathematics of compound drugs, swords). Thābit ibn Qurra: his Arabic Apollonius (Conics V) and Nicomachus, the Arabic Almagest he revised (in a manuscript transcription), and two works of his own astronomy. Ibn al-Haytham: the Optics in two OpenITI versions, Sabra's books I–III and the al-Warrāq text, and On the Configuration of the World. al-Bīrūnī: fourteen works of astronomy, mathematics and calendar, from the Masudic Canon to two fragments extant inside other treatises. ʿUmar al-Khayyām's Algebra in Woepcke's edition of 1851, two copies; its Arabic text pages stand in the scans, and the OCR reads only Woepcke's French. Held out: al-Kindī's Rasāʾil falsafiyya and Fī l-ʿaql and Fī l-nawm wa-l-ruʾyā (philosophy, outside the scientific works asked for); Thābit's Kitāb al-Rawābīʿ li-Aflāṭūn (a Hermetic work attributed to him); al-Bīrūnī's al-Jamāhir (mineralogy), al-Ṣaydana (pharmacology), Fihrist and Taḥqīq mā li-l-Hind (on India, with its astronomy inside a larger ethnography). Ibn al-Haytham's other mathematical works (on the quadrature, on Euclid's postulates) are not in OpenITI at the commits read.

license.payload: Public domain. Paul Klee died in 1940; his writings and drawings are free in every country that counts the author's life and seventy years, and both works were first published before 1931, so their United States term has run. László Moholy-Nagy, who designed the Skizzenbuch's cover and typography, died in 1946; that term has run too. The Skizzenbuch scan carries the Public Domain Mark 1.0 at the file (Internet Archive, licenseurl). The Tribüne volume is the University of Michigan copy digitized by Google: HathiTrust records the Michigan run of volumes 12–17 (1920) as pdus, public domain in the United States, full view; the Archive item carries no licence of its own. The volume's other contributors (Benn, Becher, Unruh, Felixmüller and others) are held under the same United States term, the archive's jurisdiction; some of their terms still run in Europe.

corpora.why_seated: Klee was declared wanted in the twenty-eighth seating for a reason of his own: too many files and too many image copyright landmines. The Skizzenbuch carries its drawings in the book Klee made of them, under a licence stated at the file, and the Konfession stands in the volume where it was first set beside seventeen other confessions of its moment. Seated with the exact sciences, the line that walks for its own sake stands beside the line Euclid defines as breadthless length.
corpora.scope: Held: the Pädagogisches Skizzenbuch whole, in the Bauhausbücher first printing of 1925 (Albert Langen, Munich; cover and typography by Moholy-Nagy), its figures in the scan; and the Schöpferische Konfession of 1920 in the volume that first printed it, the eighteen confessions of Tribüne der Kunst und Zeit XIII (Schickele, Pechstein, Unruh, Großmann, Klee, Toller, Benn, Hoetger, Beckmann, Scharff, Becher, Schönberg, Kaiser, Felixmüller, Sternheim, Hölzel, Marc, Däubler) bound with Bände 12 and 14–17. Not held, as the twenty-eighth seating declared them: the Jena lecture Über die moderne Kunst (1924, first printed 1945); the notebooks as Spiller edited them (Das bildnerische Denken, 1956) and the diaries as Felix Klee edited them (1957), whose editors' apparatus runs under its own terms; and the pictures, whose photographs carry their holders' claims. The Bauhaus lecture manuscripts (Bildnerische Form- und Gestaltungslehre) are digitized by the Zentrum Paul Klee; queued until a file-level licence is verified.

corpora.why_seated: Between January 1925 and January 1928 a handful of papers rebuilt the description of the atom twice, once as matrices and once as waves, and then joined both to relativity. The seat holds each in the pages where it first appeared, so that the claims later made for them can be checked against the words that made them. The European terms still run for all of them; in the United States they are already open.
corpora.scope: Held: every paper the ruling names, each in the volume or issue that first printed it: Pauli's exclusion principle (Z. Physik 31), Heisenberg's Umdeutung (Z. Physik 33), Born and Jordan (Z. Physik 34), Born, Heisenberg and Jordan (Z. Physik 35), Schrödinger's four communications (Annalen 79, 80, 81), Dirac's electron (Proc. R. Soc. A 117), and Bohr's Como lecture in its German printing (Naturwissenschaften 16). The Zeitschrift volumes are seated whole, so the same witnesses also carry the other papers of 1925–26 printed beside these. Not held: Dirac's second part, “The Quantum Theory of the Electron. Part II” (Proc. R. Soc. A 118, 1928, 351–361), not sought this session; the English printing of the Como lecture (Nature 121, 1928, supplement, 580–590), not sought; Heisenberg's uncertainty paper (Z. Physik 43, 1927, 172–198), outside the ruling's list, on the Archive under the item zeitschrift-fur-physik-vol-43 (not opened this session) and left for a later seating.

corpora.why_seated: Archimedes and Ptolemy are the two Greek authors whose demonstrations the Arabic and Latin traditions carried longest: the Sphere and Cylinder and the Sand-Reckoner on one side, the Syntaxis on the other, which the Arabs called al-Majisṭī. Heiberg edited both, and his Greek stands here beside his Euclid, already on the shelf. Thābit's Arabic Almagest stands in the Arabic seat of this seating.
corpora.scope: Ptolemy's Syntaxis (the Almagest) in Heiberg's Greek, held three ways: the First1KGreek TEI of the whole thirteen books, and the two Teubner volumes of 1898 (books I–VI) and 1903 (books VII–XIII) as scans with OCR. Archimedes in Heiberg's first edition, all three volumes (1880–81): the treatises in volumes I and II, Eutocius' commentaries in volume III, each with Heiberg's Latin. The Archive's OCR reads the Greek with errors; the loci are chosen where it reads true. Euclid is already seated (data/corpora/euclid, EA-CORPORA-20/04) and is not reseated. The First1KGreek Archimedes (tlg0552) is Mugler's Budé text of 1970–72, in copyright, and is not seated; PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit holds no Archimedes at the commit read (a6eb0cc3e6f6e382934a2c8b33577d2fb4371e00). Heiberg's second edition (1910–15) holds the Method, found in the palimpsest in 1906; its volume III (1915) is on the Archive (archimedisoperao0000jlhe) with no Greek in its OCR, and volumes I (1910) and II (1913) were not found there, so the Method is not held.

corpora.scope: The commentary on De natura hominis entire. Its preface on the joining of two short books under one title (De natura hominis and Polybus's De salubri victu) states the mechanism: in the time of the competing Attalid and Ptolemaic kings, titles and recensions were falsified by those who brought books to the kings as the writings of famous men, to receive money. Galen's other statements on Hippocratic forgery (In Hipp. Epid. and elsewhere) are not seated here.

corpora.why_seated: The prolegomena are where the tradition wrote its rules for keeping one author per name. The study reads them for what the test of genuineness presupposes, and for the mechanisms of spuriousness they name, one of which, the pupils' goodwill, describes the many writing under one.
corpora.scope: Six commentators of the school of Ammonius and its neighbours, seven texts: the commentaries on the Categories by Ammonius, Simplicius, Philoponus, Olympiodorus and Elias, Olympiodorus's Prolegomena, and David's Prolegomena to philosophy. Each prolegomenon sets the reader's questions before a treatise; one of them is whether the book is genuine, and several give the ways books came to be spurious: the ambition of royal collectors, the goodwill of pupils who wrote under the teacher's name, and homonymy of authors, of works or of commentaries. Elias names Ptolemy's catalogue of a thousand works with the life and the will. Elias's and David's commentaries on the Isagoge, and the Prolegomena of the anonymous and of Simplicius's other prefaces, are not seated.

corpora.scope: The preface entire and the list of codices that follows it. The preface is one paragraph: the Berlin Academy's plan, on Schleiermacher's initiative, to raise Aristotle 'from long neglect', the more than three years (plus quam triennium) Bekker and Brandis spent in the libraries of Italy, France and Britain, the division of labour between text and scholia, and the sigla. It says nothing of genuineness, order or authorship. The pagination this volume set (the Bekker numbers) is the one every later citation of Aristotle uses, Theophrastus's works not among them.

verified_loci: On His Own Life, fr. 2: Nicolaus a zealot of Aristotle — 'ζηλωτὴς γὰρ Ἀριστοτέλους γενόμενος'
Meyer 1841, the title: the two books of the De plantis, commonly ascribed to Aristotle, as Nicolaus's — 'NICOLAI DAMASCENI DE PLANTIS LIBRI DUO ARISTOTELI VULGO ADSCRIPTI.'
Meyer 1841, Praefatio: the book is Nicolaus's and not Aristotle's — 'Nicolai est, nec Aristotelis.'
Basel 1541, the contents: Aristotle's De plantis inside the Theophrastus volume — 'Aviftotelis De plantis, lib. 11. 198' (the page reads Aristotelis … lib. II.; the OCR reads Aviftotelis … lib. 11.)
Basel 1541, p. 267: the title — 'ΘΕΟΦΡΑΣΤΟΥ ΤΩΝ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΑ ΦΥΣΙΚΑ.'
Basel 1541, p. 271: the scholion, Nicolaus's ascription — 'Νικόλαος δὲ ἐν τῇ θεωρίᾳ τῶν Ἀριστοτέλους μετὰ τὰ φυσικὰ μνημονεύει αὐτοῦ, λέγων εἶναι Θεοφράστου'
Basel 1541, p. 271: the end of the volume's Theophrastus — 'ΤΕΛΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΘΕΟΦΡΑΣΤΟΥ.'
corpora.why_seated: Nicolaus is where the second name enters for Theophrastus's Metaphysics (draft §3.4), and a work of his own, the De plantis, travelled under Aristotle's name until Meyer restored it. The 1541 Basel volume prints the Metaphysics among Theophrastus's works, apart from Aristotle's, with the scholion still after it.
corpora.scope: Three witnesses to Nicolaus of Damascus as the scholion of Theophrastus's Metaphysics names him. (1) His fragments as Müller collected them, 165 in the DFHG, among them On His Own Life, where he is called a zealot of Aristotle (fr. 2). (2) Meyer's edition of the Latin De plantis, from Isaac ben Honain's Arabic through Alfred of Sareshel, which restores to Nicolaus the two books on plants transmitted as Aristotle's (the Greek is in Bekker's Aristotle and in the aristotle seat, tlg039). (3) The Basel Theophrastus of 1541, which the bookseller's description bound with the Archive's scan calls, after Schweiger, the first separate edition of the complete works ("Erste besondere Ausgabe der sämtlichen Werke"): it prints Aristotle's De plantis inside the Theophrastus volume (p. 198), and prints the Metaphysics as Theophrastus's (pp. 267–271) under the running heads ΘΕΟΦΡΑΣΤΟΥ and ΤΩΝ ΜΕΤΑ ΤΑ ΦΥΣΙΚΑ, the scholion after it, and ΤΕΛΟΣ ΤΩΝ ΘΕΟΦΡΑΣΤΟΥ. Nicolaus's On the Philosophy of Aristotle, which the scholion cites, survives in a Syriac compendium (Cambridge University Library, Gg. 2.14) and is edited by Drossaart Lulofs (Leiden: Brill, 1965), in copyright and declared at 32/11.

corpora.why_seated: The operator asked for all of Sappho and all the melic poets, seated with Tacitus: song and silence. Bergk's fourth edition is the last complete nineteenth-century collection of the melic fragments, public domain everywhere, in Greek with its Latin apparatus.
corpora.scope: The volume entire in session OCR, 764 PDF pages, divided at its running heads into 35 sections: Eumelus, Terpander, Alcman, Arion, Sappho, Erinna, Alcaeus, the sages' songs, Stesichorus, Ibycus, Anacreon with the Anacreontea, Lasus, Telesilla, Simonides, Timocreon, Corinna, Lamprocles, Pratinas, Diagoras, Praxilla, the Bacchylides fragments, Melanippides, Licymnius, Philoxenus, Timotheus, Telestes, Castorio, Hermodotus, the scolia, the carmina popularia and the fragmenta adespota, with the index. Pindar is in Bergk's vol. I and seated from Perseus (33/02); the papyri published after 1882 are in Edmonds (33/05) and the papyri panel (01/11).

a Sappho papyrus from Oxyrhynchus, P.Oxy. 1231, cited for the text — 'with Ox. Pap. 1231. 16 (see 15 below)' (the page abbreviates Ox. Pap.)

corpora.why_seated: Sappho is seated at one fragment (EA-CORPORA-01/10) and in the papyri panel (01/11); the operator asked for all of her. Bergk's Poetae Lyrici Graeci III (33/04) gives the fragments as known in 1882; Edmonds gives the twentieth-century papyri beside them.

verified_loci: HE 5.8.6 (Irenaeus, Adv. haer. 5.30.3, in Greek): seen not long ago, near the end of Domitian's reign — 'οὐδὲ γὰρ πρὸ πολλοῦ χρόνου ἑωράθη' (written in NFC as 'οὐδὲ γὰρ πρὸ πολλοῦ χρόνου ἑωράθη'; the seated TEI carries the oxia forms, so the locus is given in the text's own code points)

HE 3.25.4: the Apocalypse of John, 'if it seem right', which some reject and others count among the acknowledged — 'ἡ Ἰωάννου Ἀποκάλυψις, εἰ φανείη' (written in NFC as 'ἡ Ἰωάννου Ἀποκάλυψις, εἰ φανείη'; the seated TEI carries the oxia forms, so the locus is given in the text's own code points)

HE 3.28.2: Gaius on Cerinthus and revelations 'as if written by a great apostle' — 'ὁ δι᾿ ἀποκαλύψεων ὡς ὑπὸ ἀποστόλου μεγάλου' (written in NFC as 'ὁ δι᾿ ἀποκαλύψεων ὡς ὑπὸ ἀποστόλου μεγάλου'; the seated TEI carries the oxia forms, so the locus is given in the text's own code points)

HE 7.24.1: Dionysius against Nepos, bishop in Egypt — 'Νέπως ἦν, ἐπίσκοπος τῶν κατ' (written in NFC as 'Νέπως ἦν, ἐπίσκοπος τῶν κατ'; the seated TEI carries the oxia forms, so the locus is given in the text's own code points)
corpora.why_seated: The record through which the date (Irenaeus), the second John (Papias), the dispute over author and standing (Gaius, Dionysius) and the book's double entry in the ledger (3.25) reach every later stratum: strata 3.2–3.4 of Secondary Source.
corpora.scope: The ten books entire. Held for the ledger of the books (3.25), Gaius (3.28), Papias's two Johns (3.39), the Irenaeus sentence in Greek (3.18; 5.8), and Dionysius of Alexandria on Nepos and the Apocalypse (7.24–25).

verified_loci: Dio Chrysostom Or. 37.47 (Favorinus): fr. 147, 'finely said by Sappho' — 'μνάσεσθαί τινά φαμι καὶ ἕτερον ἀμμέων. πάνυ γὰρ καλῶς εἶπεν ἡ Σαπφώ'

Dio 37.47: Hesiod on undying report, and the speaker's own statue set up beside the goddess — 'φήμη δ’ οὔτις πάμπαν ἀπόλλυται, ἥντινα λαοὶ πολλοὶ φημίξωσι· θεός νύ τίς ἐστι καὶ αὐτή. ἐγώ σε ἀναστήσω παρὰ τῇ θεῷ'

Plutarch, Coniugalia praecepta 145f–146a: Sappho proud of the καλλιγραφία of her songs, writing to a rich woman — 'διὰ τὴν ἐν τοῖς μέλεσι καλλιγραφίαν ἐφρόνει τηλικοῦτον ὥστε γράψαι πρός τινα πλουσίαν'
Plutarch, Coniugalia praecepta (fr. 55, with the editor's text from 646f): no memory of you — 'κατθανοῦσα δὲ κείσεαι, οὐδέ τις μναμοσύνα σέθεν ἔσεται'
Plutarch, Quaestiones convivales 646e–f: Sappho to an unmusical and unlearned woman — 'μεμνῆσθαί μοι δοκῶ Σαπφοῦς λεγούσης πρός τινα τῶν ἀμούσων καὶ ἀμαθῶν γυναικῶν'
Stobaeus 3.4.12 (Hense): Sappho to an uneducated woman (OCR) — 'Σαπφοῦς πρὸς ἁπαίδευτον γυναῖκα'
P.Oxy. XV 1787: Sappho, Book IV (OCR) — '1787. SAPPHO, BOOK iv.'
P.Oxy. XV 1790 (Ibycus): Polycrates promised imperishable fame (OCR) — 'In the penultimate line the author addresses Polycrates, to whom he ascribes imperishable fame.'
corpora.why_seated: The ancient dossier of #1548 Part I §3 in the books that carry it. Dio's Corinthian oration (generally given to Favorinus) quotes fr. 147 with Hesiod on undying report and the speaker's own statue; Plutarch quotes fr. 55, the unremembered woman, and says Sappho was proud of the καλλιγραφία in her songs, enough to write to a rich woman; Stobaeus files the same lines under 'To an uneducated woman'; P.Oxy. XV prints Sappho's fourth book and the Ibycus poem that promises Polycrates imperishable fame. The ancient record holds remembrance claims, and the seat holds them where they stand.
corpora.scope: The carriers whole: Dio's orations, the two Plutarch treatises, Stobaeus's third book, and the papyrus volume.
